label: Population Distributions on Special Manifolds
notes: This chapter moves from the manifolds themselves to probability laws living on them. We build three population families: the uniform law as a baseline, the matrix Langevin law for directional concentration, and the matrix Bingham law for axial orientation, each anchored by modal parameters and matrix-argument normalizing constants.

label: Stiefel and Grassmann Manifolds
notes: The Stiefel manifold collects orthonormal frames of k columns in p dimensions, while the Grassmann manifold collects the k-planes those frames span. Distributions defined invariantly on the frame descend to the subspace whenever they ignore the orthogonal rotation of the frame, a recurring theme throughout the chapter.

label: The Uniform Distribution
notes: The uniform law is the unique probability measure invariant under both left and right orthogonal transformations. It is the natural null hypothesis of no preferred direction, the reference against which concentration is measured, and the limiting case every concentrated family approaches as its concentration parameter shrinks toward zero.

label: Matrix Langevin Density
notes: The matrix Langevin density is proportional to the exponential of the trace of F-transpose times X. This linear-in-X exponent generalizes the von Mises-Fisher law from the sphere to the Stiefel manifold, with the matrix F encoding both where the distribution peaks and how tightly it concentrates there.

label: Modal Orientation and Concentration
notes: Writing F through its singular value decomposition separates direction from strength. The orthogonal factors fix the modal orientation that maximizes the density, while the singular values act as concentration parameters. Larger singular values pull mass tightly around the mode; vanishing singular values return the uniform distribution.

label: Langevin: Low vs High Concentration
notes: Visualizing the circle case makes concentration tangible. With small singular values the sample scatters almost uniformly around the ring; with large values it clusters into a tight cap around the modal direction. The same contrast holds on higher Stiefel manifolds, only harder to draw cleanly.

label: Matrix Bingham Density
notes: The matrix Bingham density is proportional to the exponential of the trace of X-transpose A X, quadratic in X. Because the exponent is unchanged when any column flips sign, the law is antipodally symmetric, making it the correct model for axes and undirected orientations rather than signed directions.

label: Axial Symmetry and Eigenstructure
notes: The symmetric matrix A controls Bingham shape through its eigenvalues. Mass concentrates along eigenvectors with the largest eigenvalues and is depleted along the smallest. Adding a multiple of the identity leaves the law unchanged, so only eigenvalue differences matter, fixing the orientation up to sign.

label: Bipolar and Girdle Patterns
notes: Two eigenvalue regimes give two signature shapes. A single dominant eigenvalue produces a bipolar pattern with mass at both poles of an axis; one small eigenvalue produces a girdle of mass spread around a great circle. These patterns classify real axial data such as crystal and fault orientations.

label: Normalizing Constants
notes: Both concentrated families have normalizing constants that are hypergeometric functions of matrix argument, written with zonal polynomials. The Langevin constant is a zero-F-one in the singular values squared; the Bingham constant is a one-F-one in the eigenvalues of A. These series make moments and inference computable.

label: Computational Diagnostic
notes: The notebook samples directions on a circle and tracks the resultant length, the norm of the mean vector. Near zero it signals the uniform null; near one it signals strong concentration. This single invariant operationalizes the whole chapter, turning the abstract modal parameter into a number you can watch move.

label: Synthesis and Outlook
notes: We close by lining up the three families along one axis of structure: uniform with no preferred direction, Langevin with a signed mode, Bingham with an unsigned axis. Their modal parameters and hypergeometric constants set up the estimation, testing, and asymptotic theory developed in the chapters that follow.
